blocks.text: Recursion does not imply overlapping subproblems. The state graph here is i -> i + 1 -> ... -> len(a), with exactly one visit to each index. The index completely identifies the remaining suffix, and neither a visited set nor a memo table changes the asymptotic work. Additional state becomes justified when branching transitions can converge on the same state, as in naive Fibonacci or many grid paths. The transfer boundary is therefore call-graph overlap, not the presence of recursive syntax.

messages.text: The ordered history is derivable from the start and current i and is irrelevant to the suffix count. It makes state grow without changing the answer.
This call graph is a single chain. Each increasing index occurs once, so a visited set records facts the control flow already guarantees and does not prevent any repeated work.
Memoization is useful when the same state can be reached through multiple paths. Here each state has only one predecessor in the actual call chain, so no overlap exists.

feedback.reason: One strictly advancing child produces a chain of unique suffix states, so i is sufficient and memo state is redundant.

blocks.text: A state representation must make the current subproblem explicit. For a linked list, the node reference names the entire remaining suffix because following next reaches everything below it. The target is stable context, while a step count is irrelevant to membership. Merely defining node is None as a base case does not make an unchanged head advance toward it. This item uses termination as a diagnostic consequence, but the primary decision is state identity: choose the node that denotes the remaining structure, not the ancestor root that denotes the original problem.

blocks.text: Recursive structure alone does not determine minimal state; the result contract determines which contextual facts matter. The current nested value identifies what remains to traverse, while depth determines the multiplier applied to every leaf below it. A call on the same value at depth 2 and depth 4 has a different answer, so those states must remain distinct. By contrast, an ancestor running total is not required because each call can return its local contribution. The transfer boundary is precise: omit depth for a depth-independent aggregate such as plain sum, but retain it whenever the output or legal operation depends on nesting level.

messages.text: A full path can reconstruct the current value and depth, but it is not minimal. Passing the current value and depth names the same subproblem directly.
The running total is not needed when each call returns the contribution of its own nested value. It couples the child to ancestor history and is redundant under the stated contract.
The same nested value can contribute a different amount when reached at a different depth, so value alone collapses subproblems with different answers.

feedback.reason: Depth must be carried because it changes a leaf's contribution and cannot be derived from the current value alone.

Once l and r are present, length and the terminal condition l >= r are derivable, and the shared string remains fixed context. A different minimal convention such as (start, length) is possible, but representations must not be mixed or padded with derived fields.

blocks.text: Recursive state has two levels: its shape, such as one integer field, and its value in a particular frame. Self-similarity normally preserves the shape because each call solves the same kind of problem. Progress changes the value. Here n uniquely determines the remaining number of decrements, so adding a call counter or original input would be redundant. This distinction transfers broadly: identical parameter lists are expected; identical parameter values are suspicious when a strict progress measure should change.

blocks.text: Base cases correspond to atomic instances of the declared subproblem, not universally to empty inputs. Here every legal state denotes a non-empty suffix. The state i == len(a) - 1 identifies a singleton suffix, whose answer is already known. Because terminal status and the final value are derivable from i and the shared array, neither an empty flag nor a saved last value belongs in minimal state. The transfer rule is to define the valid recursive domain first: if emptiness is outside that domain, do not add state merely to manufacture an empty terminal case.

feedback.reason: The terminal singleton is derivable from i, so an empty-state flag adds no information and violates minimality.

blocks.text: Recursive state should contain the information that changes the meaning of the current subproblem and cannot be reconstructed from stable context. Because a is immutable and shared, i uniquely identifies a[i:]. The child state is i + 1, and len(a) is derivable from a. A running total belongs to a different accumulator-style contract, while a copied suffix represents the same state less efficiently. This boundary transfers to any shared immutable sequence: use a position or interval when it uniquely identifies the remaining region; carry extra data only when the answer truly depends on it and it is not derivable.

messages.text: The copied suffix is sufficient, but it is not minimal: i already identifies the same immutable suffix. Copying also introduces avoidable allocation and obscures the stable source array.
A mutable global cursor hides the subproblem identity outside the call. Independent calls, retries, and branching would interfere, so the state is neither explicit nor safely compositional.
A running sum describes work performed by ancestors, not the remaining suffix. It is unnecessary for a return-value contract and makes the call depend on history that the suffix itself does not need.
